1. Symptoms of the Lower Urinary Tract

  • Quote he likes (Guralnick 2011): "Similar to the lungs, the urinary bladder responds to a spectrum of pathologic processes with a limited repertoire of symptoms." So a symptom alone gives a broad differential.
Irritative symptomDefinition
UrgencySudden desire to empty the bladder
Frequency8 or more voids in 24 hours
NocturiaWaking 1 or more times at night to void
Painful voiding (older term: dysuria)Burning or stinging with urination
  • With cystitis something irritates the inside surface of the bladder, so you get these irritative symptoms (the prostate is the place to learn irritative vs obstructive symptoms).

"Urinary tract infection" by location

  • Asymptomatic bacteriuria (bacteria in normally sterile urine, no symptoms)
  • Urethritis
  • Cystitis (bladder)
  • Pyelonephritis (kidney)
  • Prostatitis
  • Urosepsis (common in forensic autopsy history: bladder infection with a pyelonephritis component leads to sepsis)

2. Diseases of the Ureter

  • Ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction: a congenital narrowing where the renal pelvis joins the ureter. The kidney keeps making urine but cannot drain it → dilated pelvis and calyces → hydronephrosis → parenchymal atrophy → possible kidney failure. Bilateral = symptoms sooner (depends on degree of stenosis). Unilateral can be silent, because one healthy kidney is enough.
  • Other congenital causes: ureteral atresia, bifid ureters.
  • Retroperitoneal fibrosis: scarring around the ureters (they run in the retroperitoneum) that encases them and causes hydronephrosis. Associated with IgG4-related disease, certain drugs, radiation, prior surgery, some malignancies (fibrotic response). Occasionally primary (Ormond disease).
  • Urothelial carcinoma: the ureter is lined by urothelium, like the renal pelvis, calyces and bladder.
Slide: papilloma of the ureter (arrow), a benign proliferation of urothelium. The renal pelvis above is not dilated, so this one is probably not significantly obstructing.
How to tell if a lesion obstructsLook upstream: a dilated renal pelvis means obstruction. A papilloma that looks like it could block the ureter but with no dilation is not.

3. Bladder Diverticula

  • Basic description: an outward pouching of the bladder wall.
  • Congenital or acquired. Acquired example: benign prostatic hyperplasia obstructs outflow → bladder distends and pressure builds → muscle hypertrophy forms trabeculae → mucosa pushes out between the bands at a weak point.
  • Often asymptomatic.
  • Complications: a pocket outside the normal flow of urine does not rinse itself, so it can become infected (recurrent UTIs) and urine there can supersaturate and form bladder stones.
Slide: bladder opened, prostate at right. Prominent muscular trabeculae show a hypertrophied, distended bladder from prostatic obstruction. The black arrow marks an acquired diverticulum.
  • A normal bladder lining is fairly smooth inside; trabeculation means outlet obstruction.
  • Congenital deformity: exstrophy = developmental defect of the anterior bladder and abdomen so the bladder opens to the outside of the body; associated with other defects.
Slide: congenital deformations of the bladder: diverticuli (congenital or acquired) and exstrophy.
Recurrent UTI? Think whyDiverticulum, stones, obstruction or reflux can all give recurrence. beyond source

4. Cystitis: Bacterial and Hemorrhagic

  • Cystitis = inflammation of the bladder. Forms: bacterial, hemorrhagic, interstitial, malakoplakia, polypoid.

Bacterial cystitis

  • The most common form of UTI.
  • Etiology: E. coli in about 90% (urethra is close to the anus, easy contamination; also the main source of pyelonephritis).
  • Symptoms: painful voiding, frequency, urgency, suprapubic tenderness, hematuria (inflamed vessels dilate and leak).
  • Urinalysis: bacteriuria and pyuria. No WBC casts (casts form in tubules, so WBC casts mean pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis).
  • Culture: in uncomplicated cases (typical female), none needed, but if done it should be positive. In a young male, think congenital anomaly and culture.
  • Pathology: hemorrhagic, discolored mucosa; neutrophils early, later macrophages and lymphocytes.
Slide: inflamed bladder, gross (bladder opened) and microscopic with inflammatory cells beneath the urothelium.

Hemorrhagic cystitis

  • Inflammation of the bladder with prominent hemorrhage.
  • Associations: cyclophosphamide (the characteristic one); adenovirus (occasionally); leukemia, DIC (bleeding tendency); severe acute bacterial cystitis.
  • Catheters can cause hemorrhage too, so interpret carefully.
Slide: hemorrhagic cystitis, gross.
Slide: hemorrhagic cystitis, gross and microscopic. Some are associated with severe acute bacterial cystitis; may be drug-related, DIC or leukemia.
Cyclophosphamide twiceIt causes hemorrhagic cystitis and is also a risk factor for bladder cancer. beyond source: the toxic metabolite is acrolein.

5. Interstitial Cystitis, Malakoplakia, Polypoid Cystitis

Interstitial cystitis (IC)

  • A chronic pain syndrome of the bladder. Broad age range, commonly females.
  • Hallmark: suprapubic pain that worsens with bladder filling and improves with emptying, so patients void often (polyuria, nocturia) to relieve pain.
  • Also urgency, frequency, hematuria, dysuria.
  • Urine culture: no growth. Urinalysis may show a few WBCs.
  • Pathology nonspecific: fibrosis (fits chronicity), mast cells (not diagnostic).
  • A diagnosis of relative exclusion. Think of it with chronic pelvic pain.
  • Side fact: an empty bladder wall can be about 1 cm thick; a full bladder wall is very thin.
Slide: interstitial cystitis. Fibrosis of the bladder wall; mast cells (arrows) with purple granules.
Slide question31-year-old woman, 3 months of painful voiding, frequency, tiny amounts of blood; negative pregnancy test; few WBCs; negative urine culture → interstitial cystitis. Acute bacterial cystitis does not fit the duration or the negative culture; hemorrhagic cystitis needs a drug, leukemia or DIC; carcinoma is unlikely at her age with no risk factors. (The original slide labeled the answer D; Dr. Kemp corrected it to E in the posted copy.)

Malakoplakia

  • Macrophages with defective phagocytic activity: bacterial products accumulate inside the cells.
  • Gross: plaque-like lesions on the mucosa (nonspecific).
  • Microscopic: sheets of foamy macrophages (big pink cells with a small nucleus) and Michaelis-Gutmann bodies: laminated, mineralized concretions (calcium salts), seen as a "bull's-eye" circle with a central dot.
  • Can occur in other organs.
Slide: Michaelis-Gutmann bodies. Left, foamy macrophages with bodies (arrows); top right, special stain highlighting them; bottom right, electron micrograph showing the laminated structure.

Polypoid cystitis

  • Inflammation causes bulbous, polypoid projections of the mucosa from submucosal edema.
  • Usually related to long-term indwelling catheters.
  • Can be confused with a urothelial neoplasm. Cystitis tends to be diffuse with multiple projections; a neoplasm is more likely a single lesion.
Slide: polypoid cystitis. Bulbous projections; submucosal edema.
Clinical reality checkMost of these specimens are autopsy cases. A cystectomy is a major, life-changing operation, so bladders are rarely removed for these benign conditions.

6. Metaplasia of the Bladder

  • Metaplasia = a relatively normal cell type that does not belong there, caused by a change in the stimulus. (Classic: intestinal-type epithelium in the esophagus from reflux.) Metaplasia → dysplasia → neoplasia is why metaplastic tissue gets biopsied.
FindingDescriptionSignificance
von Brunn nestsNests of urothelium growing downward into the lamina propriaBenign; the basis of the variants below
Cystitis glandularisNests with cuboidal or columnar epithelium forming small glandsMetaplastic process; potential risk factor
Cystitis cysticaNests with cystic spacesSame
Intestinal metaplasiaGoblet cells in the bladder liningPrecursor for adenocarcinoma (not urothelial or squamous)
Squamous metaplasiaUrothelium becomes squamous epithelium (better protection against chronic irritation: recurrent cystitis, catheter, stones)Can progress to squamous dysplasia → squamous cell carcinoma
Slide: von Brunn nests under the mucosa. The nest on the left has a central space (cystitis glandularis/cystica).
Slide: cystitis glandularis and cystitis cystica.
Slide: urothelial metaplasias. Left, squamous; right, glandular (intestinal or colonic) with goblet cells.
  • "Transitional epithelium" is the old name for urothelium. "Transitional cell carcinoma" = urothelial carcinoma.
  • He says you do not need to name the exact variant on an exam; know that metaplasia means a risk of dysplasia and neoplasia, and know squamous vs intestinal outcomes.
  • Normal urothelium has rounded surface (umbrella) cells that flatten when stretched. beyond source

7. Bladder Neoplasms: Urothelial Carcinoma

Epidemiology and risk factors

  • In the US, bladder neoplasms = 5% of cancers and 3% of cancer deaths.
  • Urothelial carcinoma: 95–97%; squamous cell carcinoma 3–7%; adenocarcinoma rare.
  • Age 50–80.
  • Risk factors: male > female; urban > rural; whites > African Americans; cigarette smoking; occupational carcinogens; cyclophosphamide; genetic; schistosomiasis (for squamous cell carcinoma).

Precursors and spectrum

  • Two precursor lesions: papilloma → invasive papillary carcinoma and carcinoma in situ (CIS) → invasive carcinoma.
LesionFeatures
PapillomaCompletely benign papillary neoplasm
Papillary urothelial neoplasm of low malignant potentialCells not quite typical, not enough to call carcinoma
Low-grade papillary urothelial carcinomaBland nuclei, few mitoses; even sizes and spacing
High-grade papillary urothelial carcinomaPleomorphic, hyperchromatic nuclei, more mitoses
Invasive urothelial carcinomaNests invade the bladder wall with fibrous reaction; into the muscle
  • Grade is based on nuclear features. Gross: exophytic (outward growing, often polypoid), which is good (grows out rather than in).
  • The higher the grade: more likely to recur, be invasive at diagnosis, progress and cause death.
  • Grading is subjective; the ends are easy, the middle is harder. Know the concepts, not exact microscopic calls.
Slide: low-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma. Papillary fronds; nuclei somewhat evenly spaced and relatively bland.
Slide: high-grade urothelial carcinoma. Exophytic mass; marked nuclear variation, hyperchromasia and mitoses.
Slide: papillary urothelial carcinoma with fibrovascular cores.
Slide: invasive urothelial carcinoma. Clusters of tumor cells in the bladder wall with fibrosis; lighter pink areas are muscle.

Carcinoma in situ

  • Gross: often not identifiable (flat).
  • Microscopic: malignant-appearing cells (pleomorphic, hyperchromatic, mitoses) that have not crossed the basement membrane.
  • If untreated, 50–75% progress to invasive carcinoma. Highly aggressive.
Slide: CIS of the bladder. Highly aggressive; flat, very pleomorphic cells that have not invaded.

Prognosis

  • Non-invasive tumor: grade is the most important prognostic feature.
  • Invasive tumor: extent of invasion and spread (stage: size, lymph nodes, metastasis) is most important.

Genetics

Slide: genetics of urothelial carcinoma.
PathwayGenetic hit
Normal urothelium → superficial papillary tumorDeletion of 9p or 9q (tumor suppressor genes)
Superficial papillary tumor → invasiveTP53 mutation
Normal urothelium → carcinoma in situTP53 mutation
CIS → invasiveDeletion of 9p or 9q
Other mutationsFGFR3, RAS and PI3K/AKT pathways, RB (with TP53 for muscle invasion)
One-line memory9p/9q loss → papillary route. TP53 → CIS route (flat, aggressive). Either route needs the other hit to invade. None of these genes is specific to bladder cancer.

Clinical presentation and treatment

  • Painless hematuria (the tumor needs blood supply, so vessels leak).
  • Diagnosis: urine cytology and cystoscopy.
  • Treatment: BCG (Bacillus Calmette-Guerin) instilled in the bladder elicits a granulomatous reaction that clears non-bulky tumor. Cystectomy if into the muscularis propria or CIS refractory to BCG.
  • Papillary tumors can recur for decades and be resected repeatedly before becoming invasive.

8. Squamous Cell Carcinoma and Schistosomiasis

  • 3–7% of bladder cancer in the US; second most common bladder cancer, far below urothelial.
  • Schistosoma haematobium infection: eggs in the bladder wall induce a reaction and squamous metaplasia → dysplasia → carcinoma. Much more common where schistosomiasis is endemic.
  • Eggs look like oval or oblong calcified structures (purple on H&E); the calcification shows on x-ray as fine punctate calcifications in the pelvis.
  • Microscopic: keratin pearls (concentric layers of keratin) and intercellular bridges are characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma.
Slide: squamous cell carcinoma related to S. haematobium. Gross mass in the bladder; egg in tissue (lower left); squamous carcinoma (lower right).
Slide: schistosomiasis. Eggs in the bladder wall, some calcified.
Slide: invasive squamous cell carcinoma with keratin pearls (arrows).
Point to ponder: SCC in the US without schistosomiasis?Most US cases have no schistosomiasis exposure. The cause is chronic irritation that produces squamous metaplasia, which becomes dysplasia and tumor. Example: a long-term indwelling Foley catheter. beyond source: also recurrent infections and chronic stones.
Slide question51-year-old recent immigrant from the Middle East, hematuria, fine punctate pelvic calcifications, biopsy shows invasive squamous cell carcinoma → schistosomiasis.

9. High-Yield Summary Table

ConditionKey points
UPJ obstructionCongenital; hydronephrosis; unilateral can be silent
Retroperitoneal fibrosisIgG4, drugs, radiation, surgery, malignancy; primary = Ormond; encases ureters
Bladder diverticulumOutpouching; BPH-acquired; recurrent UTI and stones
Bacterial cystitisE. coli ~90%; urgency, frequency, suprapubic tenderness; pyuria and bacteriuria, no WBC casts
Hemorrhagic cystitisCyclophosphamide, adenovirus, leukemia, DIC, severe bacterial
Interstitial cystitisChronic pain; worse with filling, better with voiding; culture negative; fibrosis, mast cells
MalakoplakiaDefective macrophages; foamy macrophages; Michaelis-Gutmann bodies (calcified, laminated); plaques
Polypoid cystitisEdematous bulbous projections; indwelling catheters; mimics neoplasm
von Brunn nests / cystitis glandularis / cysticaMetaplasia into lamina propria
Intestinal metaplasiaGoblet cells; adenocarcinoma precursor
Squamous metaplasiaChronic irritation; squamous cell carcinoma precursor
Urothelial carcinoma95–97%; smoking; painless hematuria; papillary (9p/9q) vs CIS (TP53) routes; BCG; cystectomy
CISFlat, high-grade, 50–75% progress
PrognosisNon-invasive: grade. Invasive: stage
Squamous cell carcinoma3–7% in US; schistosomiasis abroad; chronic irritation (Foley) in US; keratin pearls
